addressed_problems.content: The proposed Quaternion Message Passing Neural Network (QMPNN) framework and its associated mask-based Graph Lottery Ticket (GLT) discovery method are evaluated only on static graphs. However, many real-world applications involve dynamic graphs with time-varying topology or node features (e.g., social networks, traffic networks). It remains an open problem whether QMPNNs can maintain their quaternion representation efficiency and whether the lottery ticket subnetworks can adapt to evolving graph structures without full retraining. Investigating incremental update mechanisms or online pruning strategies for dynamic graphs is a necessary next step.

The QMPNN framework requires that node feature dimensions be divisible by four to form quaternion vectors, and currently handles non-multiples-of-four features by padding with average values. This approach is ad-hoc and may not preserve semantic groupings or expressive power, especially for heterogeneous graphs with categorical, textual, or image features that do not naturally split into four components. Developing principled methods—such as learned transformations, adaptive quaternion embeddings, or modality-specific preprocessing—to accommodate arbitrary and multimodal feature types is an open challenge that must be addressed to broaden the applicability of QMPNNs.

Quaternion representations in QMPNNs capture complex inter-component relationships through the Hamilton product, but the individual contributions of the four quaternion components (r, i, j, k) to the learned graph representations are not interpretable. No techniques exist to visualize or attribute which component corresponds to which semantic graph attribute, making it difficult to debug or trust the model in sensitive domains. Exploring methods for interpreting quaternion neural network decisions, such as component-wise relevance propagation or latent space visualization, remains an open future direction.

The paper empirically demonstrates the existence of winning lottery tickets in QMPNNs via iterative magnitude pruning, but it does not provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of the pruning algorithm, the optimality of the discovered masks, or the formal conditions under which lottery tickets exist in quaternion parameterizations. A rigorous theoretical analysis of the conditions (e.g., overparameterization, loss landscape properties) that ensure the existence of sparse trainable subnetworks in quaternion graph neural networks is an open problem that would strengthen the foundations of the GLT approach.

The QMPNN framework reduces parameter count via quaternion representations, but practical deployment requires optimized low-level implementations of quaternion linear algebra to fully realize memory and energy savings on specialized hardware (e.g., GPUs, edge devices). Additionally, the effect of quaternion reparameterization on training dynamics—such as convergence behavior, sensitivity to learning rate schedules, and compatibility with different optimizers (e.g., Adam, SGD)—has not been systematically studied. Addressing these engineering and optimization questions is essential for transitioning QMPNNs from research to real-world applications.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used to learn representations on graph-structured data by iteratively exchanging and aggregating messages among node neighborhoods, but several substantive gaps limited their efficiency and generality prior to this work. First, existing quaternion graph neural networks (notably the prior “Quaternion GCN”) implement quaternion algebra only for one particular GNN variant and do not provide a recipe to convert arbitrary GNN architectures into quaternion-valued counterparts; consequently, there was no general method to exploit quaternion structure across the diversity of GNN message, aggregate, and update operators. Second, prior quaternion approaches for neural networks and the existing quaternion GNN work did not realize the principal parameter-efficiency opportunity of quaternions: either they kept the original real-valued parameter counts (thereby failing to reduce model size), or they used quaternion components in a way that effectively multiplied computation and sensitivity (by letting each quaternion component operate over all input features), producing larger computational overhead and outputs that are overly sensitive to small input perturbations. Third, within the literature on sparse GNNs and graph lottery tickets, prior formulations often couple the “ticket” to pruning the input graph structure as well as model weights; this coupling renders those tickets unsuitable for graph-level tasks and for transfer learning scenarios where a pruned subnetwork must be re-used on different graphs. As a consequence of these gaps, practitioners lacked (a) a general, principled construction to obtain quaternion versions of arbitrary GNN layers that materially reduce trainable parameters while preserving the usual message-passing semantics, (b) computationally efficient quaternion GNNs that avoid inflated parameter counts and sensitivity, and (c) a formulation and algorithmic procedure to find sparse, trainable subnetworks (graph lottery tickets) for GNNs and quaternion GNNs that do not depend on pruning the input graph and that are usable for graph-level tasks and transfer learning.

nodes.content: In graph representation learning, practitioners need a systematic recipe that transforms arbitrary real-valued GNN layers (message computation, neighborhood aggregation, and state update) into quaternion-valued operations while preserving the original GNN semantics. Prior work provided a quaternion variant only for a single GNN architecture (a quaternion GCN) and therefore did not offer a way to obtain quaternion equivalents of other popular variants (e.g., GAT, GraphSAGE). Without such a general construction, researchers could not uniformly exploit quaternion algebra’s capacity to encode cross-component interactions inside a message-passing pipeline. The absence of a general mapping impeded systematic comparisons across architectures, blocked adoption of quaternion representations in models that rely on attention or sampling, and prevented development of downstream tools (e.g., quaternion-aware pruning) that must interoperate with multiple GNN families.

For energy- and memory-constrained deployment of GNNs, reducing the number of trainable parameters without worsening computational cost is crucial. Prior quaternion GNN work either left trainable-parameter counts unchanged (therefore failing to realize the parameter-efficiency theoretically available from hyper-complex representations) or used quaternion components in a way that effectively increased computational burden and sensitivity. Practitioners needed a quaternion parameterization that (a) provably reduces degrees of freedom relative to a real-weight matrix and (b) does not asymptotically increase the time complexity of the principal linear transforms performed in message-passing layers; lacking such a construction prevented the design of compact GNNs that could be trained and inferred at similar runtimes to their real-valued counterparts.

A central practical question is whether a significant reduction in trainable parameters via quaternion reparameterization can be achieved without sacrificing predictive performance across the three canonical graph tasks (node classification, link prediction, graph classification). If quaternion parameter savings require trading off accuracy, then parameter reduction would be of limited utility. Prior reports were either narrowly focused on single architectures or did not demonstrate broad empirical comparisons across tasks and datasets. Practitioners therefore lacked cross-task empirical evidence that quaternion reparameterizations can realize a large parameter reduction (≈75%) while preserving or improving task performance.

Existing graph-lottery-ticket definitions frequently tie the “ticket” to a pruned subgraph as well as to a pruned model, which is ill-suited for graph-level prediction tasks (where the whole graph’s global structure and features matter) and for transfer learning scenarios (where the same pruned subnetwork must be re-applied to different graphs). Practitioners need an algorithmic procedure that (a) searches for sparse, trainable subnetworks by masking parameters rather than removing input graph structure, and (b) returns a binary mask that yields a subnetwork that can be re-initialized to the original weights and retrained in isolation. Without such algorithms, the community lacks a practical mechanism to find compact, reusable GNN subnetworks for graph-level problems and quaternion-parameterized models.

Sparse, trainable subnetworks (lottery tickets) are valuable for reducing storage, training energy, and inference cost, but prior graph-lottery-ticket proposals either did not address quaternion-parameterized models or produced tickets that depended on pruning the input graph, limiting applicability. It was unknown whether quaternion parameterizations preserve the existence of high-performing sparse subnetworks and whether mask-based pruning (without graph pruning) could find tickets that remain performant at high sparsity on node, link, and graph tasks. Establishing the existence of such GLTs in quaternion models is necessary to justify combining quaternion parameter-efficiency with pruning for further parameter reduction.

A reduction in parameter count is only practically useful if it extends to large-scale graphs commonly used in real applications. Prior quaternion and pruning studies often reported results on small graphs or on single tasks, leaving open whether quaternion reparameterizations and mask-based sparse subnetworks generalize to large graphs used in modern benchmarks. Practitioners require evidence that parameter-efficient quaternion GNNs do not degrade when applied to large graphs (millions of edges and many nodes) and that sparse tickets produced by mask-based pruning remain effective at scale.

metadata.narrative: The generalizability of the QMPNN construction beyond the three implemented architectures (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE) is the dominant risk (P1). H1 partially mitigates this by showing that the construction works for three architecturally distinct families, proving it is not degenerate to GCN alone. However, P1's failure mode—non-linear components not covered by the specification—is not fully preempted by H1 because the paper does not explicitly describe how attention and sampling operations are converted; the methods are implemented but not formalised as a recipe. Therefore, the conclusion is credible for the three tested architectures but not fully established as a general framework covering "any" message-passing GNN. The remaining risk is that other GNN variants (e.g., GIN, MPNN with edge networks) may require additional ad-hoc modifications not provided by the current construction.

nodes.title: Quaternion Message Passing Neural Network (QMPNN) construction

nodes.content: Representing layer weights as quaternion matrices and grouping four real feature channels into one quaternion reduces the number of independent trainable real parameters by a factor of four relative to an equivalent real-valued GNN weight matrix: a quaternion weight mapping from $F$ real input features to $F'$ real outputs uses $F/4\times F'/4$ quaternion entries (each with four components shared by the Hamilton product), yielding one-fourth the degrees of freedom of the corresponding real weight matrix. At the same time, quaternion matrix multiplications implemented via the Hamilton-product block structure have the same asymptotic time complexity as the corresponding real matrix multiplications, so the parameter reduction is achieved without increasing matrix-multiplication time complexity.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified; the parameter-count reduction (factor of four) and preserved asymptotic time complexity are direct mathematical consequences of the quaternion weight matrix definition and the Hamilton product. The conclusion is sound within its own definitions and requires no empirical support. However, the practical overhead of padding features to a multiple of four is not considered a weak point because the paper addresses it by padding and shows no performance loss for real models on padded data.

nodes.title: Parameter-count reduction by quaternion parameterization with preserved time complexity

nodes.content: When QMPNN variants of standard GNN architectures (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) are trained under the same hyperparameters and evaluated on standard datasets, the quaternion models achieve comparable or better accuracy, ROC-AUC, or Hits@K (proportion of top-K predictions that are correct) while using roughly one-fourth of the trainable parameters. For example: (a) node classification on Cora: real GCN 85.2 ± 1.3 accuracy with 140.5K parameters vs QGCN 84.1 ± 1.5 accuracy with 42.1K parameters; (b) node classification on PubMed: GCN 79.1 ± 1.2 with 131.9K parameters vs QGCN 78.4 ± 1.4 with 41.7K parameters; (c) link prediction on CORA: GCN ROC-AUC 79.27 ± 0.47 with 96.0K parameters vs QGCN ROC-AUC 83.55 ± 0.03 with 27.2K parameters; (d) graph classification on MUTAG: GCN 83.54 ± 0.40 accuracy with 4.8K parameters vs QGCN 88.61 ± 0.66 accuracy with 4.4K parameters. Across all tasks and datasets evaluated, quaternion variants frequently perform within a small margin of the corresponding real models and sometimes exceed their performance while consistently having approximately one-fourth the trainable parameter count.

metadata.narrative: The main risk to the conclusion that quaternion models achieve comparable performance with one-fourth the parameters is the absence of a capacity-controlled baseline (P2). H2 provides strong statistical evidence that the observed performance across 9 datasets is not due to chance, but it does not address the missing comparison against real models with matched parameter counts. Consequently, while the paper convincingly shows that quaternion models perform competitively relative to larger real models, the implication that this constitutes a parameter-efficiency advantage over compressed real models remains untested. The conclusion holds as a descriptive fact (quaternion models perform well at 1/4 the parameters of the chosen baselines) but its interpretive strength for advocating quaternion-specific benefits is limited. The risk is that a compressed real GCN with the same parameter count would yield similar or better accuracy, undermining the claimed advantage.

nodes.title: Empirical parity or improvement of QMPNNs vs real GNNs across node, link, and graph tasks

nodes.content: A graph-lottery-ticket definition and an algorithmic procedure specialized to GNNs and QMPNNs are provided: (i) a sparsification subroutine that alternately updates model weights W and a continuous mask m via gradient steps (updating W by $W^{(i+1)} = W^{(i)} - \eta \nabla_W \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$ and updating m by $m^{i+1} = m^i - \lambda \nabla_{m^i} \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$), and finally thresholds the lowest-magnitude 20% entries of m to obtain a binary mask; and (ii) an iterative prune-rewind loop that applies the sparsification repeatedly while resetting weights to the original initialization $W^0$ to discover a binary mask m such that the masked subnetwork $f((\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}), m \odot W^0)$ is the proposed winning graph lottery ticket. This formulation explicitly avoids pruning the input graph and instead searches for sparse parameter masks, making the resulting tickets applicable to graph-level tasks and transfer learning.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified for the formulation and algorithmic procedures themselves. The redefinition of graph lottery tickets to prune only model parameters (not the input graph) is a clear conceptual contribution; the algorithms (Sparsification and Iterative Ticket Finding) are described in pseudocode and are directly implementable. The practical efficacy of these algorithms is tested in conclusion 5, and the risks there do not affect the validity of the formulation itself. The conclusion is credible as a definitional and algorithmic proposal.

nodes.title: Graph-lottery-ticket formulation and pruning algorithms for GNNs and QMPNNs

nodes.content: Winning graph-lottery tickets exist for both real-valued GNNs and QMPNNs: magnitude-based iterative pruning identifies subnetworks that match baseline performance at sparsity levels down to approximately 1–20% of the original parameter count (i.e., retaining 1–20% of weights) across multiple architectures (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) and tasks.

metadata.narrative: The existence of graph lottery tickets at high sparsity (1–20%) is supported primarily by pruning curves on three OGB datasets (H3), which provide detailed visual evidence. However, P3 identifies that the evidence does not cover the full range of datasets from the main tables and lacks a quantitative success criterion, limiting the generality of the claim. H3 partially mitigates P3 by providing a reproducible pattern for those three datasets, but the scope of the conclusion as stated—"across multiple architectures and tasks"—extrapolates beyond the dataset set. The risk is that pruning on other datasets (e.g., Cora, MUTAG) might not yield tickets at the claimed sparsity levels. The conclusion is credible for the tested configurations but not thoroughly established across the paper's full experimental landscape; a more comprehensive pruning study would be needed to confidently assert cross-task existence.

nodes.title: Existence of graph lottery tickets (GLTs) in QMPNNs at high sparsity

nodes.content: QMPNN variants scale to large graph datasets and maintain performance comparable to real-valued GNNs while using fewer parameters: on OGBN-Arxiv node classification, GCN achieves 72.8 ± 1.5 accuracy with 145.1K parameters versus QGCN 72.3 ± 1.6 with 43.5K parameters; on OGBG-COLLAB link prediction, QGCN achieves Hits@50 45.80 ± 1.35 with 6.4K parameters compared to GCN 44.02 ± 1.57 with 12.5K parameters. Thus the quaternion reparameterization is effective on large-scale graph benchmarks.

metadata.narrative: The scalability claim relies on performance on three large OGB datasets (ogbn-arxiv, ogbl-collab, ogbg-molhiv). P4 points out that this test bed is limited in both graph size and feature dimensionality relative to the full OGB suite. Without highlights that extend the scope or analyze scaling behavior (e.g., runtime vs. graph size, memory usage, or results on ogbn-products), the conclusion's validity is bounded to the tested regime. The conclusion is a plausible inference from the data, but the evidence is insufficient to confirm that QMPNNs scale to the most challenging large graphs commonly used in the field. The risk is that on graphs with millions of nodes or high-dimensional features, padding or memory overhead may cause performance degradation not seen in the tested cases.

nodes.title: QMPNNs scale to large graphs while preserving performance

nodes.content:
The QMPNN construction only specifies quaternion replacements for linear feature transforms; non-linear message computations such as attention coefficient scoring in GAT (which involves dot products and softmax) and LSTM-style updates are not addressed. Therefore, the claim that the MESSAGE, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE functions of any message-passing GNN can be replaced by quaternion counterparts is not generally proven and is only validated for the three architectures (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE) for which experiments are conducted.
      Eq. (5), Eq. (6)

metadata.failure_mode: If the construction cannot be extended to non-linear components in an architecturally faithful way, then the conclusion that it maps any real-valued GNN to a quaternion GNN fails, because many GNNs (e.g., GAT, GraphSAGE with max-pooling) rely on such operations. The claim of a "general" construction would be reduced to a specific recipe for simple linear transforms, and the QMPNN approach would be limited to architectures without complex non-linear message functions. Moreover, the evaluation only covers GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE, so failure to generalise to other variants (e.g., GIN, MPNN with edge networks) remains untested, narrowing the scope of the conclusion.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper describes only the Hamilton product for linear transformations and does not specify how to convert attention-weight computation, sampling procedures, or other non-linear operations to quaternion arithmetic in a generic way. The claim of a "generalizable framework" relies on an implicit assumption that any operation can be replaced by its quaternion analog without further specification. This assumption is unsupported because operations like attention scoring depend on dot products between feature vectors, which are replaced by quaternion dot products or Hamilton products; the paper does not analyze whether the resulting attention distribution preserves the intended semantics.

nodes.title: Generality of QMPNN construction not fully specified

nodes.content:
The empirical evaluation compares quaternion GNN variants (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) to their real counterparts with the same number of hidden units and four times the trainable parameters; no comparison is made against real GNNs with the same parameter count (obtained by reducing hidden dimension). Therefore, the observed comparable or better accuracy of quaternion models at roughly one-fourth the parameters does not separate the effect of the quaternion parameterization from the general possibility that reducing parameters does not degrade accuracy on the tested datasets. The parameter-efficiency advantage of the quaternion representation relative to compressed real models is untested.
      Table 3, Table 4, Table 5

metadata.failure_mode: If a real GNN with the same number of parameters as the quaternion model (achieved by reducing hidden dimensionality) achieves performance similar to or better than the quaternion model, then the conclusion that quaternion models are parameter-efficient relative to real models is undermined. The claim would be that quaternion models perform well with few parameters, but that might be a property of the task rather than of quaternion space. The conclusion would remain true as a statement of fact (the quaternion model performs well with few parameters), but its interpretation as an argument for quaternion advantage would be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: A proper evaluation of parameter efficiency requires comparing models with the same number of parameters to isolate the effect of quaternion representation from the effect of reduced capacity. Without such a baseline, the reported performance parity could simply indicate that the datasets are not sensitive to model capacity, rather than demonstrating a structural advantage of quaternion algebras. The paper does not provide experiments that control for trainable parameter count by reducing the hidden dimension of the real GNN, which is the standard way to test parameter efficiency.

nodes.title: Missing capacity-controlled baseline in empirical comparison

nodes.content:
Winning graph lottery tickets at 1–20% of original model size are demonstrated via magnitude pruning only on three datasets (ogbn-arxiv for node classification, ogbl-collab for link prediction, ogbg-molhiv for graph classification) and a subset of architectures; pruning results are not reported for all datasets used in the main tables, no quantitative criterion is provided for "match baseline performance" (e.g., within one standard deviation), and the prune fraction (0.3 per iteration) and learning rate schedule are fixed without sensitivity analysis. Therefore, the existence claim is not fully established across tasks, architectures, and hyperparameter settings.
      Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the missing pruning experiments on other datasets (e.g., Cora, Citeseer, MUTAG) show that tickets do not exist or exist only at much lower sparsity, then the general claim that GLTs exist at 1–20% sparsity across multiple architectures and tasks would be contradicted. Even if tickets exist on the three tested datasets, the conclusion's implied generality would be invalid if other datasets break the pattern. The failure would narrow the conclusion to a specific set of benchmarks rather than the claimed cross-task existence.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that "GLTs exist at 1/5th or smaller of original size" is supported only by pruning curves for three out of the nine datasets used elsewhere. The paper does not define what constitutes "winning" in terms of a quantitative threshold (e.g., performance within 1% of baseline), leaving the assessment subjective. Additionally, the prune fraction (retaining 70% after each iteration until reaching the target sparsity) is not varied; alternative schedules might change which tickets are found. Without more extensive evidence, the claim that GLTs exist broadly across tasks and architectures is only weakly supported.

nodes.title: Limited evidence for GLT existence across tasks and architectures

nodes.content:
The evaluation of QMPNN scalability to large graphs is conducted on three OGB datasets (ogbn-arxiv, ogbl-collab, ogbg-molhiv) with feature dimension 128 and moderate graph sizes (up to ~236K nodes, ~2.4M edges for ogbl-collab); no experiments are performed on the largest OGB graphs (e.g., ogbn-products with ~2M nodes and 256 features, ogbl-ppa with large edge count). Therefore, the conclusion that QMPNNs scale to large graphs while preserving performance is not validated beyond the tested regime, leaving open whether the parameterization scales to graphs with very high node counts or high-dimensional features that are not multiples of four without significant performance degradation.
      Table 3, Table 4, Table 5

metadata.failure_mode: If QMPNNs are applied to graphs like ogbn-products and fail to maintain performance or training stability (e.g., due to padding inefficiency or memory constraints), the conclusion that they "scale to large graphs" would be false for the most demanding cases. The conclusion would be restricted to datasets with ≤2.4M edges and features that are either already divisible by 4 or small enough that padding overhead is negligible. The claimed scalability would not hold in the most practically relevant large-scale settings.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper tests QMPNNs on three datasets that, although large, do not represent the full range of graph sizes and feature dimensionalities found in OGB. For example, ogbn-products has 2,449,029 nodes and 256-dimensional features; ogbl-ppa has 42.8M edges. The paper does not test on these more challenging graphs. Additionally, the largest feature dimension among tested datasets is 128, which is divisible by 4; it is unknown whether padding to achieve divisibility harms performance on graphs with high-dimensional features (e.g., 300 features would require padding to 304). Thus, the claim of scaling is an extrapolation from a limited set of conditions.

nodes.title: Scalability evaluation limited to three large datasets

nodes.content: For three standard GNN architectures (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE), the paper provides concrete implementations of quaternion-valued counterparts (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) using the described Hamilton product transformation, and demonstrates through experiments that these models can be trained with standard stochastic gradient descent, achieving comparable performance to the original real-valued models across node, link, and graph classification tasks on multiple datasets.

metadata.credit: Without this empirical demonstration, the claim that "any message-passing GNN can be mapped to a quaternion version" would rest solely on an abstract recipe with no evidence of viability for non-trivial architectures. The successful implementation and training of three architecturally distinct models (GCN, which uses symmetric normalization; GAT, which relies on attention; GraphSAGE, which uses sampling and various aggregators) shows that the Hamilton product transformation can be incorporated into diverse message-passing pipelines. This reduces the risk that the construction fails for non-linear operations (the dominant concern raised in P1) by providing existence proofs for three families that employ precisely those non-linearities. The conclusion gains credibility for these architectures, though not yet for all possible GNNs.

nodes.title: Empirical validation on three architecturally distinct GNN families

nodes.content: The evaluation of real and quaternion GNNs spans 9 datasets (Cora, Citeseer, PubMed, OGBN-Arxiv, MUTAG, PROTEINS, ENZYMES, OGBL-COLLAB, OGBG-MOLHIV) across the three fundamental graph tasks, with each configuration run over 5 random seeds and the reported performance quantified by mean and standard deviation. The paper further applies paired t-tests to determine whether differences between models are statistically significant.

metadata.credit: This controlled statistical methodology preempts the common criticism that a single train/test split or a few runs could produce misleadingly favorable results for quaternion models. By showing that quaternion models are often statistically indistinguishable from or better than real models across a diverse set of datasets, the credibility of the conclusion that the parameter reduction does not harm performance is substantially increased. The pattern is reproducible and significant, even though the missing capacity-controlled baseline (P2) limits the conclusion about parameter-efficiency advantage. The statistical rigor ensures that the observed parity is not due to random fluctuation.

nodes.title: Broad and statistically rigorous empirical comparison

nodes.content: Figure 2 in the paper plots test accuracy/AUC/Hits@50 against the fraction of remaining parameters for GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE on three OGB datasets (ogbn-arxiv, ogbl-collab, ogbg-molhiv), marking the point at which the pruned subnetwork matches or nearly matches the baseline with a star. The curves show a plateau region where performance remains near baseline even as sparsity increases to the 1–20% range.

metadata.credit: The visual evidence preempts the vulnerability that the GLT existence claim rests only on summary numbers or unaveraged runs. The curves demonstrate a gradual degradation rather than a cliff edge, and the markers explicitly identify conditions under which the pruned subnetwork meets baseline performance. This strengthens the claim for the tested datasets by providing a reproducible quantitative pattern and showing that the tickets are not isolated points but emerge from a continuous sparsity-performance trade-off. Although P3 notes that the evidence does not cover all datasets, for the three OGB datasets the curves provide a level of detail that is more informative than a single statistic.

nodes.title: Detailed pruning curves with explicit winning-ticket markers

steps.reasoning: Define a graph $\mathcal{G} = \{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}\}$ where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of vertices and $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of edges; define the node feature vector for node $v\in\mathcal{V}$ at layer $l$ as $h_v^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^F$, where $F$ is the number of real-valued feature channels per node. This notation is used to express standard message-passing GNN computations where MESSAGE, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE are layerwise functions that compute messages $m_{uv}$, aggregate neighbor messages, and update node states respectively.

Introduce quaternions: denote the set of quaternions by $\mathbb{H}$ and represent a quaternion $q$ as $q = q_r + q_i \mathrm{i} + q_j \mathrm{j} + q_k \mathrm{k}$ with real-valued components $q_r,q_i,q_j,q_k\in\mathbb{R}$ and imaginary units $\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}$ satisfying $\mathrm{i}^2=\mathrm{j}^2=\mathrm{k}^2=\mathrm{ijk}=-1$. Define quaternion addition component-wise and quaternion multiplication by the Hamilton product $q\otimes p$, which can be implemented by a $4\times4$ real block matrix acting on the four real-component vectors of the multiplicands.

Require that the number of real feature channels $F$ is divisible by $4$ so that every node feature vector can be grouped into $F/4$ quaternion entries: define the quaternion feature vector for node $v$ at layer $l$ as $h_v^{(l),Q} = h_r^{(l)} + h_i^{(l)}\mathrm{i} + h_j^{(l)}\mathrm{j} + h_k^{(l)}\mathrm{k}$, where $h_r^{(l)},h_i^{(l)},h_j^{(l)},h_k^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{F/4}$ are the real and three imaginary component subvectors obtained by partitioning the original $F$ real channels into four equal groups.

Represent layer parameters in quaternion form: for each learnable layer $l$, define the quaternion weight matrix $W^{(l),Q} = W_r^{(l)} + W_i^{(l)}\mathrm{i} + W_j^{(l)}\mathrm{j} + W_k^{(l)}\mathrm{k}$, where $W_r^{(l)},W_i^{(l)},W_j^{(l)},W_k^{(l)}$ are real-valued component matrices of compatible dimensions (specifically mapping $F/4$ quaternion input channels to $F'/4$ quaternion output channels when the real-valued analog maps $F$ to $F'$).

Preserve message-passing semantics by replacing each real-valued MESSAGE, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE function with quaternion-valued counterparts that perform their internal linear transforms and nonlinearities using the quaternion representation just defined: explicitly, whenever a GNN layer would compute linear transforms via real weight multiplications on $h_v^{(l)}$, the quaternionized layer instead computes the analogous transforms using $W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q}$ and carries out aggregation and update operations over quaternion component vectors, so the layerwise message-passing structure (compute messages, aggregate neighbor messages, update node state) is retained in quaternion space.

Note compatibility with existing GNN variants: because the construction replaces only the internal representation of feature vectors and the linear transforms (weights) by their quaternion analogues and implements the Hamilton product by the block real-matrix form above, the same procedure applies to different MESSAGE designs (e.g., attention-based message computations in GAT or sampling-based neighborhood summaries in GraphSAGE) by substituting their linear components with quaternion linear components. This provides a systematic recipe to obtain quaternion-valued versions of arbitrary message-passing GNN layers.
[8]

Start from the QMPNN construction established earlier (conclusion 1): quaternion features are formed by grouping every four real channels into one quaternion entry, and quaternion layer weights are represented as $W^{(l),Q}=W_r^{(l)}+W_i^{(l)}\mathrm{i}+W_j^{(l)}\mathrm{j}+W_k^{(l)}\mathrm{k}$ with the Hamilton-product block structure implementing linear transforms.

Compare parameter counts: consider a real-valued linear mapping from $F$ real input features to $F'$ real outputs represented by a real weight matrix of size $F\times F'$, containing $F\times F'$ independent real parameters. For the quaternion parameterization, group the $F$ input channels into $F/4$ quaternions and the $F'$ output channels into $F'/4$ quaternions; the quaternion weight matrix then contains $(F/4)\times(F'/4)$ quaternion entries.

Translate quaternion entries into real degrees of freedom: each quaternion entry conceptually has four real components $(\cdot)_r,(\cdot)_i,(\cdot)_j,(\cdot)_k$, but these components are structured and shared in the Hamilton product via the block matrix in which the same component matrices $W_r^{(l)},W_i^{(l)},W_j^{(l)},W_k^{(l)}$ interplay to produce outputs. Thus the total number of independent real-valued trainable parameters in the quaternion parameterization is $(F/4)\times(F'/4)\times 4 = (F\times F')/4$, which is one-fourth the number of parameters of the equivalent real-valued weight matrix.

State this as a factor reduction: therefore representing layer weights as quaternion matrices and grouping four real feature channels into one quaternion reduces the number of independent trainable real parameters by a factor of four relative to an equivalent real-valued GNN weight matrix.

Address computational time complexity: note that the Hamilton-product-based quaternion matrix multiplication is implemented by the real block matrix multiplication shown previously (a $4\times4$ block matrix whose blocks are the component real matrices). Block-matrix multiplication of that form can be carried out using a fixed constant number of real matrix multiplications and additions whose asymptotic time complexity, as a function of input and output dimensions, matches that of the corresponding real matrix multiplication up to constant factors. Therefore, implementing the quaternion linear transforms via the Hamilton-product block structure does not increase the asymptotic time complexity of the principal linear operations compared to the real-valued counterparts.

Conclude that parameter reduction is achievable without worsening asymptotic matrix-multiplication cost: combine the reduction in degrees of freedom (one-fourth) with the preserved asymptotic computational cost to assert that the quaternion parameterization yields one-fourth the independent real parameters while not increasing the time complexity of matrix multiplications performed in message-passing layers.

Start from the QMPNN construction (conclusion 1) as the model family evaluated: the quaternion variants (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) are obtained by replacing linear components with quaternion weights and grouping four real channels into one quaternion as previously described.

Describe the experimental protocol used to compare quaternion models to real-valued baselines: the experiments use the same architectures (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE vs QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) with identical hyperparameters and training setups (two- or three-layer models with 128 hidden units as appropriate, learning rate $0.01$, weight decay $5\times10^{-4}$, dropout $0.6$, Adam optimizer, up to 1000 epochs with early stopping after 200 epochs of no improvement, and evaluations averaged over five random seeds with means and standard deviations reported); dataset preprocessing for quaternion models pads features/classes to be divisible by 4 when necessary.

Present representative numeric results from the reported tables that demonstrate empirical parity or improvement while using roughly one-fourth of parameters: (a) node classification on Cora: real GCN achieves $85.2\pm 1.3$ accuracy with $140.5$K parameters versus QGCN $84.1\pm 1.5$ accuracy with $42.1$K parameters; (b) node classification on PubMed: GCN $79.1\pm 1.2$ with $131.9$K parameters versus QGCN $78.4\pm 1.4$ with $41.7$K parameters; (c) link prediction on CORA: GCN ROC-AUC $79.27\pm 0.47$ with $96.0$K parameters versus QGCN ROC-AUC $83.55\pm 0.03$ with $27.2$K parameters; (d) graph classification on MUTAG: GCN $83.54\pm 0.40$ accuracy with $4.8$K parameters versus QGCN $88.61\pm 0.66$ accuracy with $4.4$K parameters. These numeric comparisons are reported in the experimental result tables.
Table 3, Table 4, Table 5

Explain statistical treatment and fairness of comparison: each reported value is the mean and standard deviation computed over five random seeds; paired t-tests are used to determine statistically significant differences and the models are trained under identical hyperparameters and data splits (for node classification an 80-10-10 split, for link prediction and graph classification an 85-5-10 split), ensuring that the comparisons isolate the effect of quaternion parameterization.

Synthesize the empirical claim: across the full set of reported experiments (node classification, link prediction, and graph classification on multiple datasets), quaternion variants are frequently within a small margin of the corresponding real models and sometimes exceed their performance while consistently having approximately one-fourth the trainable parameter count, demonstrating that substantial parameter reduction need not entail a loss of predictive performance.

State the goal: find sparse, trainable subnetworks (winning graph lottery tickets) for GNNs and quaternion GNNs that do not prune the input graph structure and that can be re-initialized and retrained in isolation; define a mask vector $m\in\mathbb{R}^{\|W\|}$ applied elementwise to model parameters via the Hadamard product $\odot$, so a masked network has parameters $m\odot W$ (or $m\odot W^Q$ for quaternion weights).

Provide a sparsification subroutine (denote it Algorithm 1) that alternately updates model parameters $W$ and a continuous mask $m$ by gradient steps: update model weights by gradient descent $W^{(i+1)} = W^{(i)} - \eta \nabla_W \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$, where $\eta$ is the step size and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$ is the task loss; update the continuous mask by gradient descent $m^{(i+1)} = m^{(i)} - \lambda \nabla_{m^i} \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$, where $\lambda$ is the mask step size. After a fixed number of iterations, convert the continuous mask to a binary mask by thresholding the smallest-magnitude $p\%$ entries of $m$ to zero and setting the rest to one, producing a sparsified binary mask.

Provide an iterative prune-rewind loop (denote it Algorithm 2) that repeats the sparsification step and rewinds weights to their original initialization $W^0$: initialize a binary mask $m^0=\mathbf{1}$, then iterate: (a) apply the sparsification subroutine to the current masked network; (b) update the mask according to the sparsification outcome; (c) reset the network weights to the initial weights $W^0$ (rewinding); (d) continue until the desired sparsity level $s$ (i.e., $1-\frac{\|m\|}{\|W\|}=s$) is achieved. The output is a binary mask $m$ such that the subnetwork $f((\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}), m \odot W^0)$ is the proposed winning graph lottery ticket.

Explicitly avoid pruning the input graph: the algorithms operate solely by masking model parameters $W$ (or quaternion parameters $W^Q$) and never remove edges or vertices from the input graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X})$, ensuring that the discovered tickets are applicable to graph-level tasks where the entire graph structure and features matter and are suitable for transfer learning to different graphs that should be processed by the same masked subnetwork.
[1]

Define the quaternion variant of the graph-lottery-ticket procedure by applying the same sparsification and iterative prune-rewind algorithms to quaternion-parameterized models: given a QMPNN $f(\cdot, W^Q)$, run the sparsification (Algorithm 1) and iterative loop (Algorithm 2) with quaternion-valued weights and quaternion input features to find a binary mask $m$ so that $f(\cdot, m\odot W^{Q,0})$ is the quaternion winning ticket; the mask $m$ is defined over real-valued parameter entries (or over quaternion component parameters as implemented) but the procedure does not rely on pruning the input graph.

Treat as known the graph-lottery-ticket formulation and algorithms that operate by masking parameters and iteratively pruning and rewinding (conclusion 4); treat as known the QMPNN construction (conclusion 1) that provides quaternion-parameterized model families on which to run the pruning algorithms.

Specify the pruning procedure used empirically: apply magnitude-based iterative pruning (the iterative prune-rewind procedure implemented as Algorithm 2 together with the sparsification updates of Algorithm 1) to both real-valued GNNs and QMPNNs; the pruning procedure repeatedly sparsifies parameters by setting the smallest-magnitude fractions of mask entries to zero, rewinds weights to initialization, and repeats to reach progressively higher sparsity levels while monitoring validation/test performance.

Report empirical findings from pruning experiments across architectures and tasks: the experiments show that magnitude-based iterative pruning identifies subnetworks whose performance matches the baseline dense models at sparsity levels retaining approximately $1\%$ to $20\%$ of the original parameter count (i.e., subnetworks that are $1$–$20\%$ the size of the original model) across multiple architectures (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) and tasks (node classification, link prediction, graph classification). This empirical range is reported in the paper's key findings and is visualized in the pruning-vs-performance plots.
Fig. 2

Describe how the plots support the claim: the pruning plots (performance after pruning) display performance curves as a function of retained parameter fraction and mark winning graph-lottery tickets (GLTs) with star symbols (red and green stars) at points where the pruned subnetwork attains performance comparable to the pre-pruning baseline despite high sparsity; these visual markers and the corresponding numeric table entries corroborate that GLTs exist at retention levels in the $1\%$–$20\%$ range.
Fig. 2

Cross-check with tabular results: the result tables for node classification and link prediction show parameter counts and performance numbers for quaternion and real models, and the pruning experiments reported in conjunction with those tables indicate that the pruned subnetworks at the stated sparsity levels maintain comparable performance; the paper highlights this observation as a key finding and supports it with Table 3 and Table 4 entries and the pruning visualization.
Table 3, Table 4

Conclude existence of GLTs in quaternion models: combining the use of the mask-based iterative pruning algorithms (which do not prune the input graph) with the empirical pruning curves and tabled performance, assert that winning graph-lottery tickets exist for both real-valued GNNs and QMPNNs at high sparsity (retaining roughly $1$–$20\%$ of original parameters) across the evaluated architectures and tasks.

Start from the QMPNN construction (conclusion 1) as the method applied to large-graph datasets: quaternion reparameterization groups features into quaternions and replaces linear transforms with quaternion Hamilton-product-based transforms implemented by the real block-matrix form described earlier.

Identify large-scale benchmark datasets used in experiments and their sizes: for example, the OGBN-Arxiv node-classification dataset has $169{,}343$ nodes and $1{,}166{,}243$ edges with $128$ features per node, and OGBL-COLLAB (ogbbl-collab) for link prediction has $235{,}868$ nodes and $2{,}358{,}104$ edges with $128$ features; these dataset statistics are part of the experimental dataset summaries used to evaluate scalability.
Table 1

Present representative numerical comparisons on large benchmarks showing preserved performance with fewer parameters: on OGBN-Arxiv node classification, GCN attains $72.8\pm 1.5$ accuracy with $145.1$K parameters while QGCN attains $72.3\pm 1.6$ accuracy with $43.5$K parameters; on OGBL-COLLAB link prediction, QGCN attains Hits@50 $45.80\pm 1.35$ with $6.4$K parameters compared to GCN Hits@50 $44.02\pm 1.57$ with $12.5$K parameters. These figures are reported in the experimental result tables for large datasets.
Table 3, Table 4, Table 5

Explain experimental protocol and infrastructure confirming practical scalability: the same training hyperparameters and optimization settings are used (learning rate $0.01$, weight decay $5\times10^{-4}$, Adam optimizer, early stopping) and experiments are executed on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs with 24GB VRAM; the reported GFLOPs (gigaflops) and parameter counts in the tables indicate that quaternion models reduce parameter counts substantially while retaining similar computational footprints for the principal linear operations.

Conclude that quaternion reparameterization is effective at scale: because QMPNN variants deliver comparable accuracy/Hits@K on large-scale benchmarks while using significantly fewer parameters (empirically observed on OGBN-Arxiv and OGBL-COLLAB among others), QMPNNs scale to large graphs while preserving performance, demonstrating practical applicability of the quaternion parameter-efficiency to real-world, large-graph tasks.

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges several unresolved scientific and engineering directions left open: (1) The adaptability of the QMPNN construction and the proposed mask-based GLT discovery to dynamic graphs (time-varying topology or features) is untested and remains to be developed. (2) Hybrid modalities and multimodal graph inputs (heterogeneous node/edge feature types that do not naturally split into four-component quaternion groupings) pose representational and preprocessing challenges not addressed here; methods to handle non-multiples-of-four features beyond simple padding require investigation. (3) Interpretability of quaternion feature interactions and how quaternion components map to semantically meaningful graph attributes is unexplored; techniques to visualize or attribute quaternion-component contributions remain future work. (4) While the algorithms demonstrate mask discovery by iterative magnitude-based sparsification, the paper does not provide theoretical guarantees on convergence, optimality of masks, or formal conditions under which winning tickets exist in quaternion parameterizations; formal analysis of when and why GLTs exist for QMPNNs is left open. (5) Practical deployment questions—such as optimized low-level implementations of quaternion linear algebra for reduced memory and energy on specialized hardware, and the effect of quaternion reparameterization on training dynamics across a wider set of optimizers and schedules—are not resolved and are proposed directions for future research.
